title: Maximum Sum BST in Binary Tree
description: Brute force to optimized: separately validating and summing each subtree versus a single combined post-order bundle per node.

sections.title: Maximum Sum BST in Binary Tree

content.title: Maximum Sum BST in Binary Tree

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given a binary tree (not necessarily itself a valid BST), find the maximum sum of node values among all subtrees that ARE valid binary search trees. If no subtree is a valid BST, return 0.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","root of a binary tree"],["Output","The maximum sum among all subtrees that are valid BSTs (0 if none)"],["Key Insight","A single post-order pass can report, for every node, whether its subtree is a valid BST, its min and max values, and its sum, all simultaneously"],["Constraints","Up to 4*10^4 nodes"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Find the best VALID subtree matching a structural property, summed\"","A post-order recursion returning a compact bundle of information per node (validity, min, max, sum), letting each node combine its children's bundles into its own in O(1)"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

A subtree rooted at a node is a valid BST exactly when both its children's subtrees are ALSO valid BSTs, AND the current node's value is strictly greater than the maximum value in its left subtree, AND strictly less than the minimum value in its right subtree. If all of this holds, the current subtree's own sum, min, and max can be computed directly from its children's already-known sum, min, and max, letting a running best answer be updated as this recursion proceeds.

blocks.title: Analogy: Certifying Valid Organizational Sub-Units, Then Totaling Their Budgets
blocks.text: Picture certifying whether an organizational sub-unit forms a valid, properly ordered hierarchy, which is only possible if BOTH of its child sub-units are themselves already validly ordered AND the sub-unit's own leader fits correctly between them; a validly certified sub-unit's total budget can then be compared against the best certified budget seen so far.

blocks.caption: Each node reports (is this a valid BST, its min, its max, its sum) simultaneously, combining its children's reports

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: tree = [1, 4, 3, 2, 4, 2, 5, null, null, null, null, null, null, 4, 6]
Maximum BST subtree sum = 20.
5. How Should We Think?

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Validating whether a subtree is a BST, and separately computing its sum, are both properties that can be determined RECURSIVELY from the SAME children's information, so they should be combined into a single pass rather than computed separately.

Observation 2: Define dfs(node) to return a bundle: (is this subtree a valid BST, the minimum value in it, the maximum value in it, its sum of values). An empty (null) node is trivially a valid BST with sum 0, and needs carefully chosen sentinel min/max values (positive/negative infinity) so it never incorrectly restricts a parent's validity check.

Observation 3: A node's subtree is a valid BST exactly when both children report valid BSTs, AND the node's own value exceeds the left subtree's max, AND is less than the right subtree's min.

Observation 4: When a node is confirmed a valid BST, its own sum (left sum plus right sum plus its own value) can immediately be compared against a running global best; if NOT valid, that subtree, and every subtree containing it, can no longer be considered a candidate (though ancestors might still find OTHER valid BST subtrees elsewhere).
This leads to a single post-order recursion, where each node combines its children's (validity, min, max, sum) bundle into its own, updating a running best sum whenever a valid BST subtree is found.
6. Brute Force Solution
For every node in the tree, separately and independently validate its ENTIRE subtree as a BST from scratch (a fresh recursive check), and separately compute its sum if valid.
Why the code is written this way

items: Separately validating and summing each subtree from scratch directly implements the definition.
This recomputes the SAME work repeatedly across nested, overlapping subtrees, costing O(n squared) worst case; combining validity, bounds, AND sum into one post-order pass avoids all this repetition.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) worst case (a skewed tree), due to repeated full re-validation and re-summation.
Space: O(h) recursion depth per call.
Limitation: a single post-order pass, returning a compact bundle per node, computes validity, bounds, and sum simultaneously, with no repeated work.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Define dfs(node) returning a tuple (isBst, subtreeMin, subtreeMax, subtreeSum). For a null node, return (true, positive infinity, negative infinity, 0) as sentinels that never incorrectly constrain a parent. Otherwise, recursively get the left and right bundles. If both children report isBst true, AND node.val is strictly greater than the left bundle's max, AND strictly less than the right bundle's min, this subtree is a valid BST: compute its sum (left sum plus right sum plus node.val), update the running global best with this sum, and return (true, min(left min, node.val), max(right max, node.val), sum). Otherwise, return (false, irrelevant placeholder values...) to signal this subtree (and anything containing it) is not a valid BST.
Use a single post-order recursion returning a compact (validity, min, max, sum) bundle per node, updating a running global best whenever a valid BST subtree is found.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run intuition (partial, for the given example tree)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Node region","Bundle reported"],"rows":[["Leaf nodes with no children","(true, val, val, val), trivially a valid single-node BST"],["A node whose value fits strictly between its valid children's bounds","(true, combined min, combined max, combined sum), updates the running best"],["A node violating the BST ordering, or with an invalid child","(false, ...), disqualifies this subtree and everything containing it from being counted"]]}

codes.python:
def max_sum_bst(root):
    best = 0
    def dfs(node):
        nonlocal best
        if node is None:
            return True, float('inf'), float('-inf'), 0            # sentinel: never restricts a parent
        l_is_bst, l_min, l_max, l_sum = dfs(node.left)
        r_is_bst, r_min, r_max, r_sum = dfs(node.right)
        if l_is_bst and r_is_bst and l_max < node.val < r_min:
            total = l_sum + r_sum + node.val
            best = max(best, total)                                  # update running global best
            return True, min(l_min, node.val), max(r_max, node.val), total
        return False, 0, 0, 0                                        # disqualified
    dfs(root)
    return best

blocks.text: Why This Works

Bundling validity, bounds, and sum together into a single post-order return value means every node combines its children's ALREADY-COMPUTED information in O(1), rather than re-deriving it from scratch; the sentinel values for null nodes (infinite min, negative infinite max) correctly ensure an empty subtree never accidentally restricts its parent's BST validity check, and updating the running global best exactly when a subtree is confirmed valid correctly captures every candidate exactly once.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), each node processed exactly once.
Space: O(h) recursion depth.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Separately validate and sum each subtree from scratch","O(n squared) worst case","O(h) per call","Correct, but redundant repeated work."],["Single post-order pass, combined bundle per node","O(n)","O(h) recursion depth","The expected, efficient solution."]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
Maximum Sum BST in Binary Tree is a strong example of combining MULTIPLE pieces of information (validity, bounds, sum) into a single recursive bundle, avoiding redundant separate passes.
Common Mistakes

items: Validating BST-ness and computing the sum as two entirely SEPARATE recursive passes per node, causing the redundant O(n squared) cost.
Using incorrect sentinel values for null nodes (for example, using 0 instead of positive/negative infinity for min/max), which can incorrectly disqualify or validate a parent subtree.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["No subtree (other than possibly single nodes) is a valid BST","Every single node alone is trivially a valid BST, so the answer is at least the maximum single node value."],["The entire tree is already a valid BST","The answer is simply the sum of all node values."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "combine validity, min, max, and sum into ONE recursive return value, computed once per node" demonstrates the key efficiency insight clearly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "find the best VALID subtree matching a structural property", think: a post-order recursion returning a compact combined bundle per node, avoiding redundant separate passes.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you also report WHICH subtree (its root node) achieves the maximum sum, not just the sum itself?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Validate Binary Search Tree, whose recursive bounds-checking idea is directly incorporated here as part of the combined bundle.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The separate-validation-and-summing approach costs O(n squared) worst case; the single combined post-order pass costs O(n), the standard efficient solution.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: a single post-order recursion returning a combined bundle (validity, min, max, sum) per node.
Core Idea: a subtree is a valid BST exactly when both children are valid BSTs and the node's value strictly fits between their bounds; valid subtrees' sums are compared against a running global best.
Time: O(n squared) worst case for the brute force, O(n) for the combined single-pass approach.
Most Important Observation: combining multiple related properties into one recursive bundle avoids redundant separate computations.
Interview Difficulty: a hard problem combining BST validation with an optimization objective.
One line memory trick: one bundle per node: valid, min, max, sum, all at once.
